interest: This file provides rare, candid insight into the technical and ecological foundations of U.S. Occupation policy in Japan, specifically the tension between demilitarization and economic self-sufficiency. Authored by prominent Harvard geographer Dr. Edward A. Ackerman for SCAP's Natural Resources Section, the enclosed interpretive summary offers an extraordinarily sophisticated carrying-capacity analysis, explicitly connecting Japan's democratic prospects to resource conservation, energy development, and population control. Most notably, the document contains frank discussions on the necessity of Japanese birth control (declaring that without it, 'death control is likely to enter'), warns against treating emigration as a viable demographic safety valve, and forcefully lobbies the Allied powers and the Far Eastern Commission against punitive industrial stripping or excessive reparations, demonstrating how resource experts sought to moderate Allied policy to avert ecological collapse and social unrest.
overview: This file (894.508/2-748) documents the completion and diplomatic transmission of 'Japanese Natural Resources--A Comprehensive Analysis,' a landmark monograph prepared by Dr. Edward A. Ackerman and Louis M. Richard, Jr. of the Natural Resources Section of General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (GHQ/SCAP). Filed under the State Department decimal file for Japanese conservation of natural resources, the bundle includes a Department of State record copy replacement form, Despatch No. 79 (dated February 7, 1948) from Acting U.S. Political Adviser W. J. Sebald to the Secretary of State, a general outline of the monograph's contents (Enclosure 1), and an advance copy of Section III, the 'Interpretative Summary' (Enclosure 2), alongside duplicate filing copies of the despatch's first page and the summary. The core report provides a comprehensive, data-driven assessment of Japan's post-World War II resource predicament, documenting severe structural deficits in food, timber, liquid fuels, coking coal, and industrial minerals for a population projected to reach 80 to 90 million. It argues that achieving a peaceful, democratic society requires not only rigorous domestic conservation, industrial efficiency, and urgent population stabilization through birth control, but also enlightened Allied policies, including minimal industrial restrictions, access to Asian raw materials and export markets, expanded fishing grounds, and a reparations program that does not destroy Japan's capital base.

It replaces the original action copy, which was not returned to Central Records by the action office. The form instructs personnel not to detach it and mandates return to DC/R for permanent filing under decimal file number 894.508/2-748.

subfiles.about: A diplomatic despatch transmitting an overview and summary of a SCAP study on Japanese resources and urging its immediate publication and circulation.
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald, Acting Political Adviser, Office of the United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Acting Political Adviser William J. Sebald reports that the Natural Resources Section of GHQ/SCAP is completing 'Japanese Natural Resources--A Comprehensive Analysis,' authored by Dr. Edward A. Ackerman with cartography supervised by Louis M. Richard, Jr. Prior to Ackerman's return to Harvard University, he briefed Northeast Asian Affairs Chief John M. Allison and mission staff on the report's extensive data regarding severe domestic shortages in food, wood, liquid fuels, and industrial minerals. Sebald summarizes the report's key findings on Japan's foreign trade difficulties and necessary conservation measures, strongly recommending that the State Department support immediate publication and wide distribution to Far Eastern Commission member nations.

subfiles.to: George C. Marshall, The Secretary of State, Washington

subfiles.about: A detailed structural outline of the chapters and sections comprising SCAP's comprehensive analysis of Japanese natural resources.
subfiles.from: Natural Resources Section, General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.summary: This enclosure provides the complete topical outline of the three sections making up the Natural Resources Section's comprehensive analysis. Section I outlines Japan's resource base and material requirements, spanning food, agriculture, fisheries, electric power, coal, petroleum, fibers, construction materials, and minerals. Section II details avenues for increasing productive efficiency through improved processing, conservation, substitution, and scientific research. Section III is listed as the Interpretive Summary synthesizing the economic and geopolitical implications.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 1 to Despatch No. 79: Outline of 'Japanese Natural Resources--A Comprehensive Analysis'

subfiles.about: An interpretive policy summary analyzing Japan's severe resource deficiencies, the necessity of population stabilization, and recommended Allied economic policies.
subfiles.from: Dr. Edward A. Ackerman, Technical Adviser, Natural Resources Section, General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.summary: This summary presents a sobering diagnosis of Japan's economic future, calculating that an anticipated population of 80 to 90 million will require massive permanent imports of food, timber, petroleum, fertilizer minerals, and industrial metals. Because export prospects are severely constrained by regional fears, postwar shortages, and global competition, Japan cannot rely solely on foreign trade to balance its accounts. The author argues that Japan must aggressively pursue internal conservation, technological modernization, and domestic population stabilization through birth control rather than futile hopes of emigration. Furthermore, it urges the Allied powers to foster democratic stability by keeping industrial restrictions minimal, allowing light metal and synthetic manufacturing, avoiding reparations from critical production or power facilities, and granting expanded access to regional fishing grounds.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 2 to Despatch No. 79: Section III, Interpretative Summary of 'Japanese Natural Resources--A Comprehensive Analysis'

subfiles.about: The initial page of a duplicate copy of Despatch No. 79 regarding the SCAP Natural Resources Section report.
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This document is the opening page of a duplicate filing copy of Despatch No. 79 from Tokyo, stamped with State Department classification markings 894.508/2-748. It recounts the preparation of the Natural Resources Section report by Dr. Edward A. Ackerman and Louis M. Richard, Jr., and describes their meeting with John M. Allison. The page sets forth the initial objectives of the report concerning Japan's productive capacity in food, fuel, and raw materials before breaking off at the end of the sheet.

subfiles.to: George C. Marshall, The Secretary of State, Washington

subfiles.about: A duplicate text of the 12-page Interpretative Summary of the SCAP report on Japanese resource limitations and Allied occupation policy.
subfiles.from: Dr. Edward A. Ackerman, Technical Adviser, Natural Resources Section, General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.summary: This sub-file consists of a duplicate copy of the complete twelve-page Interpretative Summary (Section III) of the SCAP Natural Resources Section study. It outlines the stark structural deficits confronting Japan's expanding population in food, forest products, energy, and minerals, emphasizing that technical improvements alone cannot outpace population growth without deliberate birth control. The text concludes with specific recommendations for Allied occupation authorities, counseling against punitive reparations and excessive industrial controls while encouraging trade access and expanded fishing grounds to secure a stable economic foundation for democracy.
